chapter_theme: After an invocation and a verse offering the book as rain against famine, the chapter counts things under one predicate (amrita, beauty, laughable, poison, painful, death, the tongue's death) across the household, the king's service and a Jain code whose crown is not being born again by giving up lying, theft, women and meat.

0.reading: The poet bows without fault to the feet of the one who knew everything, put away the three and does not age, praises him fully, and says he will tell some venbas of firm use to the people of the world.
0.nuance: The one praised is named only by three attributes (all-knowing, rid of the three, ageless) and by no deity's name; the verse does not say what the three are.

1.reading: The verse calls on its hearers to tell the Sirupanchamoolam as a rain that ends a great famine, setting out fitting conduct and setting aside the four that are not to be done: killing, lying, meat and theft.
1.nuance: The verse puns on பஞ்சம் (famine) inside the title's பஞ்ச மூலம். The four are read from கொலைபோய் புலால்களவோ(டு) with போய் taken as பொய் (a lie); ஓர்நால் counts these four, and ஒத்த ஒழுக்கம் is the frame they serve, not a fifth item. Lines 1-2 are hard to construe.

items.claim: killing is one of the four the book sets aside
lying is one of the four the book sets aside
eating meat is one of the four the book sets aside
theft is one of the four the book sets aside

2.reading: Enjoyment lies with the man who has wealth and dharma with the man who has grace, and the man of grace does no blameworthy deed, does not come near sin and does not carry backbiting to others' ears.
2.nuance: Divided into five: two possessions, then three refusals of the gracious man. Wealth gets one clause and grace the rest of the verse.

items.claim: enjoyment belongs to the man who has wealth
dharma belongs to the man who has grace
the man of grace does no deed that earns blame
the man of grace does not come by sin
the man of grace does not carry backbiting into others' ears

3.reading: A chaste woman, a man who has learned and is restrained, a land of good surroundings, a king whose banner reaches the clouds and who is good to his land, and a soldier who does his work as it should be done are each named amrita.
3.domain_note: three of the five belong to the realm: land, king and soldier
3.nuance: Only the soldier is amrita on a condition (ஆகவே செய்யின், if he does it rightly). Line 3's மேகமே may instead name the rain cloud as a separate amrita for the land, which would make six things; we read it as the height of the king's banner.

items.claim: a chaste woman is amrita
a man who has learned and become restrained is amrita
a land with good surroundings is amrita
for the land, a good king whose banner touches the clouds is amrita
a soldier is amrita if he does his service as it should be done

4.reading: The subtlety an unlearned man thinks he has found, a proud carriage of the neck by a woman who lacks both ears, and a man with nothing saying he gives unattainable wealth to the needy and is generous are, the verse says, laughter to the good when they hear of them.
4.nuance: Three things, not five; all three are claims that outrun what the person has, so the laughter is at pretension, not at lack. காதிரண்டும் இல்லாதாள் may mean a woman without ears or without ear ornaments.

items.claim: the fine point an unlearned man thinks he sees is laughable to the good
a woman lacking both ears holding her neck proudly is laughable
a man with nothing claiming to give unattainable wealth to the needy is laughable

5.reading: The verse says that one who would be rid of the body should practise high penance, one who would end want here should give, one who would be rid of folly should learn, and one who does not desire another man's wife will gain fortune.
5.nuance: Read as four counsels with fortune (திரு) as the closing reward, so four items. இடம்பொழிய and மடம்பொழிய are hard to divide, and அறிமடம் may be one word (feigned ignorance) rather than அறி plus மடம்; the third item is our best construal. Ending the body means not being born again.

items.claim: high penance is the means for one who would be rid of the body
giving is the means for one who would end want here
learning is the means for one who would be rid of folly
not desiring another man's wife brings fortune

6.reading: Elephants are the beauty of an army, slenderness the beauty of a woman's waist, unbending speech the beauty of conduct, the same unbending the beauty of the sceptre, and unwavering courage the beauty of soldiers.
6.nuance: கோடா (not bending) is used once and carried by அதுவே to the sceptre, so truthful speech and just rule are made one quality.

items.claim: elephants are the beauty of an army
slenderness is the beauty of a woman's waist
speech that does not bend is the beauty of conduct
not bending is likewise the beauty of the king's sceptre
courage that does not wilt is the beauty of soldiers

7.reading: The verse defines five titles by conduct: the ascetic is one who holds to the book of the one free of attachment, the leader is one who has mastered every matter, the பார்ப்பான் is one who shares his food out of devotion, the worthy man is one who is aware of blame, and one who eats with care sees no disease.
7.nuance: பார்ப்பான் is a word for the brahmin by birth; here the verse defines him by an act, sharing food, not by birth. Lines 1-2 are missing from the site's text, and பற்றினான் may also be read with the brahmin (holding to the primal one's book).

items.claim: the ascetic is one who holds to the book of the one free of attachment
the leader is one who has mastered every matter
the brahmin is one who shares his food out of devotion before eating
the worthy man is one who is aware of what brings blame
one who guards his eating does not meet disease

norm.note: a varna term defined by conduct: the verse names who counts as a பார்ப்பான் by sharing food

8.reading: Kindly regard is the beauty of the eye, not going where one should not the beauty of the feet, saying exactly how much the beauty of reckoning, the hearers' saying 'good' the beauty of music, and the people's saying it is good that he does not oppress his land the beauty of a great king.
8.nuance: The last two beauties are both a judgment by others (கேட்டார் நன்று என்றல், நன்று என்றல்): the song and the king are beautiful by what listeners and subjects say.

items.claim: kindly regard is the beauty of the eye
not going where one should not is the beauty of the feet
stating exactly how much is the beauty of reckoning
the hearers' saying 'good' is the beauty of music
the people's praise that he does not oppress his land is the beauty of a king

9.reading: The tongue dies, the verse says, in one who kills and eats, in one who goes as a false witness, in the unlearned before those who know the good, in a debtor when he sees even once, and in the well-born when he has eaten and comes to know of it.
9.nuance: The tongue's death is losing the power to speak for shame. கடவான் is read as the debtor (one who owes) facing his creditor, and the last item as the well-born man struck dumb on learning what or from whom he has eaten; both construals are ours.

items.claim: the tongue of one who kills and eats dies
the tongue of one who goes as a false witness dies
the tongue of the unlearned dies before those who know the good
the tongue of a debtor dies when he sees even once
the tongue of the well-born dies when he has eaten and comes to know it

10.reading: Its own eggs are death to the spider, its long horns death to the beast, its hair death to the animal that cannot turn, its own young death to the crab, and words of abuse death to the tongue.
10.nuance: Each creature is killed by something of its own; the list sets abuse beside them, so the tongue's ruin comes from itself, not from the one abused.

items.claim: its own eggs are death to the spider
its long horns are death to the beast
its hair is death to the animal that cannot turn
its own young are death to the crab
abuse that is not good is death to the tongue

11.reading: The worth of a man without shame, the vow of a man without conduct, the generosity of a man without food, the soldiering of a man without strength and the verse-making of one who does not know good Tamil are laughable, the verse says, when weighed by speech.
11.nuance: Each item is a virtue claimed by one who lacks its ground. The fifth turns the book's ridicule on poets.

items.claim: the worth claimed by a man without shame is laughable
the vow of a man without conduct is laughable
generosity done by a man who has no food is laughable
soldiering by a man without strength is laughable
verse-making by one who does not know good Tamil is laughable

12.reading: Killing is poison, enjoying meat is a cruel poison, overcoming one who is no match is poison, harming at length one who trusted is poison, and speaking ill of a young girl without inquiry is poison.
12.nuance: Only eating meat gets the stronger கொடுநஞ்சு, so the verse ranks eating above killing. நஞ்சூனைத் fuses நஞ்சு and ஊனை. மா(று) அல்லானை is read as 'one who is no match'; நீடாங்கு செய்தல் and இளங்கிளியை (a young parrot, or a girl addressed as one) are doubtful.

items.claim: killing is poison
enjoying meat is a cruel poison
overcoming one who is no match is poison
harming at length one who trusted is poison
speaking ill of a young girl without inquiry is poison

13.reading: Distress among friends is painful, not giving is painful, ties with those who are not friends are painful, the suffering of the pure is painful, and, the poet tells a woman, a vow taken and left short is painful.
13.nuance: கண்டல் அவர் in line 3 is hard to place; read with the fourth item it makes it 'seeing the suffering of the pure'. The address பூங்கதுப்பினாய் (you of the flowered hair) is the frame, not an item. Three things are fused with இன்னா in the text, so their `thing` carries it as written.

items.claim: distress that befalls friends is painful
not giving is painful
ties with those who are not friends are painful
the suffering of the pure is painful to see
a vow taken and left short is painful

14.reading: The verse names as the virtue of each: for a woman, walking the way of the man who married her; for a son, following his father's way without fail; for kin, the same; for soldiers, not leaving the hot front of spears; and for a king's land, living by his sceptre.
14.nuance: Every item is a following: wife after husband, son after father, soldier at the front, people under the sceptre, so the verse makes one virtue of keeping to one's place in an order.

items.claim: for a woman, walking the way of her husband is virtue
for a son, following his father's way without fail is virtue
for kin, the same following is virtue
for soldiers, not leaving the hot front of spears is virtue
for the king's land, living by his sceptre is virtue

norm.note: a rule of women's conduct of the period: the wife is to walk her husband's way

15.reading: Bearing with a wrong is greatness, sitting brooding on harm done is smallness, and it is good to live so that the enmity one made comes to an end and so that the wealthy and the good have no cause to laugh.
15.nuance: Four items, not five: two set greatness against smallness, two name a good way of living. பல்பொருளார் நல்லார் may be read as the subjects (the wealthy and good, living so none laugh at them) rather than the ones who laugh.

items.claim: bearing with a wrong is greatness
brooding on harm done is smallness
living so that enmity one caused ends is good
living so that the wealthy and good have no cause to laugh is good

16.reading: Before people without worth, anger is good, nobility bad and arrogance good, the verse says, for goodness shown there is like good meat in the mouth of a dog that bit and rose barking.
16.nuance: Three items, the inversion of the house virtues made explicit (கதம் and மதம் are fused with நன்று in the text); the closing image says kindness spent on the base is wasted like meat in a dog's mouth. Line 3 (கோய்வாயிற் கீழுயிர்க்(கு)ஈ துற்று) is hard to construe.

items.claim: anger is good before people without worth
nobility is bad before people without worth
arrogance is good before people without worth

17.reading: Making friends, humbling enemies, lying with broad-hipped women of sharp teeth, and keeping love for those within one's house are named the fruit gained by a body that has not renounced.
17.nuance: Four fruits, all of the unrenounced body (துறவா உடம்பு), so the verse grants the householder's life its gains while marking them as the lesser body's. ஓட்டித் தொடங்கினார் is doubtful.

items.claim: making friends is a fruit of the unrenounced body
humbling enemies is a fruit of the unrenounced body
lying with broad-hipped women of sharp teeth is a fruit of the unrenounced body
love within one's house is a fruit of the unrenounced body

18.reading: One who does not lie though he would gain gold, does not steal, does not turn to soft women though long-haired women want him, does no harm, and, knowing the body will leave, does not eat flesh out of craving, will hardly take a body again.
18.nuance: The reward is not this world's but release from rebirth (பேர்த்துடம்பு கோடல் அரிது). Each abstention is set against its strongest temptation (gold, women who desire him). வையாமை and நையாமை are uncertain: we read 'not setting on' and 'not afflicting'.

items.claim: not lying even for gold leads away from rebirth
not stealing leads away from rebirth
not turning to women though they desire him leads away from rebirth
doing no harm leads away from rebirth
not eating flesh out of craving leads away from rebirth

19.reading: Those who have learned are gods and the unlearned, on examination, ghouls; those who did not earn wealth early are wretches; and those who say they had no sorrow before and were the handsome ones are two-legged oxen.
19.nuance: Four items. The scale runs from god to ghoul to beast, and the last item mocks those who live on their past.

items.claim: those who have learned are gods
the unlearned are ghouls
those who did not earn wealth early are wretches
those who boast of past ease and beauty are two-legged oxen

20.reading: One who does not steal, never gives himself to gambling, does not befriend the black-hearted, does not move his tongue to take life, and refuses meat will never, worn out, take on a body of flesh again.
20.nuance: The line division கள்ளான்கு தென்றும் is read as கள்ளான் சூது என்றும். The closing pun sets the refused flesh (ஊன்) against the flesh-body (ஊனுடம்பு): refusing the one, he is not given the other.

items.claim: one who does not steal escapes rebirth
one who never gives himself to gambling escapes rebirth
one who does not befriend the black-hearted escapes rebirth
one who does not use his tongue to take life escapes rebirth
one who refuses meat escapes rebirth

payiram.reading: The payiram says that Makkariyasan, pupil of Makkayan, whose hand is like rain ending the other famine of not learning, made the Sirupanchamoolam to remove the ills of many in the world.
payiram.nuance: It joins the title's two senses: the five roots as medicine (நோய்நீக்கும்) and பஞ்சம் as famine, here the famine of the unlearned (கல்லா மறுபஞ்சம்).

links.note: Verse 1 offers the book as rain that ends a great famine; the payiram calls the author's hand rain that ends the famine of not learning.
links.teaches: Together they show the famine pun is the book's own gloss on its title: the five roots cure, and the rain they bring is learning.

links.note: Verse 1 names killing, lying, meat and theft as the four the book sets aside; verse 20 lists theft, gambling, bad company, harmful speech and meat as what frees one from a flesh body.
links.teaches: The preface's four abstentions are, by verse 20, the price of release from rebirth, so the book's opening ethic is already a soteriology.

links.note: Kural 247 says that world is not for those without grace as this world is not for those without wealth; verse 2 gives enjoyment to wealth and dharma to grace, then spells out grace as three refusals.
links.teaches: Where the couplet only assigns grace its world, the verse says what grace does here: it refuses blame, sin and tale-bearing, so grace is chiefly a restraint of deed and tongue.
links.list_adds: It pairs wealth and grace as the first two items and then gives grace three more, so the list tips the balance the couplet keeps even.

links.note: Both counted works place the chaste wife first among things that heal: Thirikadugam calls her shoulders part of a medicine, Sirupanchamoolam calls her amrita.
links.teaches: In both works the wife's chastity heads a list whose other items are public goods (worthy company, learned friends; land, king, soldier), so the household virtue is ranked as a good of the realm.

links.note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's wish to speak to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood; verse 4 sets the unlearned man's subtlety beside the pride of a woman lacking both ears.
links.teaches: The two share an old figure of the unlearned as a body lacking its marks, but the verse splits the simile into two separate objects of laughter and adds a third, the poor man's boast.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's single simile into a list of three pretensions, so the woman's pride is no longer a figure for the unlearned but a ridiculous thing of its own.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 13 says the fine point an unlearned man has found is hard for him to show, so he should not rate himself among the good; verse 4 says that same subtlety makes the good laugh.
links.teaches: Read together, the pair gives both the cause and the effect: the unlearned man's insight cannot be shown, and so to the learned it is merely comic.

links.note: Kural 150 says that even one who does wrong does well not to desire another's wife; verse 5 promises fortune to one who does not desire her.
links.teaches: The couplet values the restraint even without other virtue; the verse makes it the gate to fortune, so the same act is moved from a minimum of decency to a source of gain.
links.list_adds: It sets not desiring another's wife beside penance, giving and learning as four means to four ends, so this restraint is ranked as one of the means of a whole life.

links.note: Kural 546 says victory comes from the unbending sceptre, not the spear; verse 6 makes the unbending its beauty and gives the army elephants and the soldier courage.
links.teaches: The couplet sets the sceptre against force; the verse keeps both, giving force its own beauties and joining the sceptre's straightness to truthful speech by one word, கோடா.
links.list_adds: It gives the sceptre the same quality as unbending speech and sets it among the army's and soldiers' beauties, so justice is ranked with force instead of against it.

links.note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous who wear kindness to every creature; verse 7 says the பார்ப்பான் is the one who shares his food.
links.teaches: Both define a priestly title by conduct rather than birth, and the verse makes the conduct a concrete daily act, sharing food, where the couplet names a disposition.
links.list_adds: It defines the brahmin in a row with the ascetic, the leader and the worthy man, so the birth title is treated as one more role earned by an act.

links.note: Kural 134 says a பார்ப்பான் can relearn the Veda but his birth is ruined when conduct fails; verse 7 defines the பார்ப்பான் by sharing food alone.
links.teaches: The couplet keeps birth and makes conduct its condition; the verse drops birth from the definition, so the verse goes further than the Kural in detaching the title from birth.
links.list_adds: By listing the brahmin with titles anyone can earn, the list removes the birth the couplet still assumes.

links.note: Kural 575 calls kindly regard the eye's only jewel; verse 8 calls it the eye's beauty and gives four other members their beauties.
links.teaches: The couplet stops at the eye; the verse runs the same 'X's beauty is Y' through feet, reckoning, song and king, so the last two beauties are other people's praise.
links.list_adds: It sets the eye's beauty in a series that ends with a king judged by his people, so kindly regard becomes the first of a scale from the body to rule.

links.note: Kural 403 says the unlearned are good if they can keep silent before the learned; verse 9 says the unlearned man's tongue dies before those who know the good.
links.teaches: The couplet makes silence a choice that redeems; the verse makes it a shame that strikes, so the same silence is a virtue in one and a punishment in the other.
links.list_adds: It sets the unlearned man's mute tongue beside the killer's, the false witness's and the debtor's, so ignorance is ranked with guilt as a cause of shame.

links.note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue like begging, even water for a cow; verse 9 says the well-born man's tongue dies when he has eaten and knows it.
links.teaches: Both place the shame of dependence in the tongue; on our reading of the verse, eating from the wrong hand silences the well-born as begging degrades the asker.
links.list_adds: It sets the well-born man's shame beside the debtor's, so the list treats owing and being fed as one kind of silencing.

links.note: Kural 127 says to guard the tongue above all, or suffer through faulty words; verse 10 says abuse is death to the tongue as its own eggs are to the spider.
links.teaches: The couplet warns of the speaker's suffering; the verse's animals show why: the harm grows from the speaker's own body, as a creature is killed by its own young or horns.
links.list_adds: It sets abusive speech last after four creatures killed by their own parts or offspring, so the tongue's ruin is shown as self-made.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 39 calls liberality in a man who has nothing to give painful; verse 11 calls the generosity of a man without food laughable.
links.teaches: The two name the same thing from two sides: painful to the would-be giver and laughable to the onlooker, so empty generosity fails both inwardly and in public.

links.note: Kural 1014 says shame is the ornament of the worthy and without it a proud walk is a disease; verse 11 says the worth of a shameless man is laughable.
links.teaches: Both deny worth without shame, but the verse makes the failure social ridicule where the couplet makes it a sickness of the man himself.
links.list_adds: It sets shameless worth among four other claimed virtues without ground (vow, generosity, soldiering, poetry), so shame is shown as the ground the others also need.

links.note: Kural 254 says grace and its absence come down to not killing and killing, and eating that flesh is not right; verse 12 calls killing poison and eating meat a cruel poison.
links.teaches: The couplet derives the wrong of eating from killing; the verse ranks eating as the worse poison, so the eater is held more guilty than the killer.
links.list_adds: It grades the two acts with நஞ்சு and கொடுநஞ்சு, a ranking the couplet does not make.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 22 calls eating flesh to swell one's flesh painful before all else; verse 12 calls enjoying meat a cruel poison.
links.teaches: Both counted works single out meat-eating with a stronger word than their other items (முன்னின்னா, கொடுநஞ்சு), so the ranking is shared across the group.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 25 opens with seeing a friend's troubles as painful; verse 13 opens with distress among friends as painful.
links.teaches: Both works put a friend's distress first among painful things, but Sirupanchamoolam pairs it with not giving, so the pain is also a call to help.

links.note: Kural 55 praises the wife who worships her husband, not a god, and commands the rain; verse 14 makes walking her husband's way a woman's virtue.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the wife's devotion cosmic power; the verse sets the same following among son, kin, soldier and subjects, as one case of keeping one's place.
links.list_adds: It lists the wife's following with the son's, the soldier's and the people's, so the rule for women is presented as one form of a general duty of following.

links.note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the ruler's sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 14 calls living by the sceptre the virtue of the king's land.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks of the king's duty to the people's need; the verse turns it into the people's virtue, obedience to the sceptre.
links.list_adds: It counts living by the sceptre among household and military duties, moving it from the king's chapter into the subject's code.

links.note: Kural 152 says bear with excess and better still forget it; verse 15 calls bearing a wrong greatness and brooding on harm smallness.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks forgetting above bearing; the verse names brooding as the opposite of forgetting and calls it smallness, so it supplies the failure the couplet leaves implied.
links.list_adds: It sets greatness and smallness as a contrasting pair and adds ending enmity as a third good, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Kural 303 says forget anger at anyone at all, since evils are born of it; verse 16 says anger is good and nobility bad before people without worth.
links.teaches: On the plain reading of verse 16 the two disagree about the same act: the Kural allows no exception to forgoing anger, while the verse makes the base an exception.
links.list_adds: It inverts three house virtues at once (anger, nobility, pride) for one audience, so the exception is a rule, not a lapse.

links.note: Naladiyar 70 says no one bitten by a dog bites it back, so the high do not answer the low in kind; verse 16 uses a barking dog to say goodness to the base is wasted and anger is good.
links.teaches: Both use the dog for the base man and draw opposite counsels: the Naladiyar asks for restraint, the verse for anger and pride.
links.list_adds: It sets anger and pride as good beside nobility as bad, so the list reverses the Naladiyar's ranking of forbearance above response.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 40 calls fierceness in a man of self-restraint painful; verse 16 says anger is good before people without worth.
links.teaches: The pair marks a limit: fierceness is unfitting in the restrained man in general, but Sirupanchamoolam carves out the base as the one place it serves.

links.note: Verse 17 names lying with women and keeping house as the fruits of the unrenounced body; verse 18 says not turning to women who want him is a way out of rebirth.
links.teaches: The book grants the householder's body its fruits but sets the higher reward, not being born again, on giving up exactly those fruits.

links.note: Kural 260 says all creatures worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; verse 18 says one who does not eat flesh out of craving will hardly take a body again.
links.teaches: The couplet's reward is honour in this world; the verse's is release from the body, so the same abstention is given a Jain soteriological fruit.
links.list_adds: It joins refusing meat to truth, honesty and chastity, each tested by its strongest temptation, as joint conditions of release.

links.note: Verses 18 and 20 both close a list of abstentions, meat last, with the promise that one will not take a body again.
links.teaches: The book states the same Jain promise twice in three verses, with meat as the final condition each time, which shows how central diet is to its idea of release.

links.note: Kural 410 says others are to the learned as beasts are to people; verse 19 calls the learned gods and the unlearned ghouls.
links.teaches: The couplet uses one step, beast to human; the verse widens the scale to god and ghoul and saves the beast for the boaster, so learning is placed on a three-step ladder of beings.
links.list_adds: It sets learning beside early earning and against nostalgic boasting, ranking each as god, ghoul, wretch or ox.

source_issues: Verse 1 line 1: கொலைபோய் is read as கொலை பொய் (killing, lying); போய் is likely a misprint for பொய்.
Verse 7: show flags that the site's text lacks lines 1 and 2; their construal is uncertain.
Verse 8 line 4: நஞ்றென்றல் is likely a misprint for நன்றென்றல், as in line 3.
